qigong.e: From the Hanyu Pinyin romanization of Mandarin 氣功 /气功 (qìgōng, “breath work, qi work”).
qigong.x: My patients laud qigong as a stressbuster and cure for pesky chronic symptoms that baffle doctors.

quack.e: From Middle English *quacken, queken (“to croak like a frog; make a noise like a duck, goose, or quail”), from quack, qwacke, quek, queke (“quack”, interjection and…
quack.x: Did you hear that duck make a quack?

quadrant.e: Inherited from Middle English quadrant, from Old French cadran, quadrant and its etymon Latin quadrāns, -antis (“fourth part of something, quarter”). Doublet of quadrans.
quadrant.x: Ops wanted some initiative, blew up their entire quadrant. I'm movin' like Oppenheimer.

quadratic.e: From French quadratique (1765), from Latin quadrātus + -ique (English -ic), form of quadrō (“to make square”), from quādrus (“square”), ultimately from…

quadrilateral.e: Learned borrowing from New Latin quadrilaterus + -al.
quadrilateral.x: The Venetian quadrilateral comprised Mantua, Peschiera, Verona, and Legnano.

quadrille.e: French, in sense of “group of knights”, from Spanish cuadrilla, diminutive of cuadra (“square”) (compare also cuadra (“four”)), from Latin quadra.

quadruple.e: From Middle English quadruple, from Latin quadruplus. Can be analyzed as quadri- + -ple.
quadruple.x: Our profits quadrupled when we made the improvements.

quagmire.e: Recorded since 1579, from quag + mire. The sense “perilous, mixed up and troubled situation” has been recorded since 1775.
quagmire.x: The paperwork got lost in a quagmire of bureaucracy.

quail.e: From Middle English quayle, quaile, quaille, from Anglo-Norman quaille, from Late Latin quaccola (“quail”).
quail.x: Quail require little water, so there is no point to putting in a guzzler if there is any permanent water within travel range.

quaint.e: From Middle English queynte, quoynte, from Anglo-Norman cointe, queinte and Old French cointe (“pretty, clever, knowing”), from Latin cognitus, past participle of…
quaint.x: I admire all that quaint, old-fashioned politeness; it is much more to my taste than modern ease; modern ease often disgusts me.

qualification.e: Borrowed from Middle French qualification in the 1540s, which in turn derives from Medieval Latin quālificātiō. By surface analysis, qual(ify) + -ification.
qualification.x: Qualification for this organization is extraordinarily difficult.

qualified.x: Assuming that I have all the information, my qualified opinion is that your plan will work.

qualify.e: Borrowed from Middle French qualifier (“to qualify”). Equivalent to quality + -fy.
qualify.x: But if it is done in conjunction with repointing of the building, the work would probably qualify as a major capital improvement.

qualitative.e: From Late Latin (or Medieval Latin) quālitātīvus. Equivalent to quality + -ative.
qualitative.x: You may recall that I made a qualitative post about our level 100 talents a little more than a month ago. Now let’s look at them qualitatively.

qualm.x: This lawyer has no qualms about saving people who are on the wrong side of the law.

quantitative.e: From Late Latin quantitātīvus. By surface analysis, quantity + -ative.
quantitative.x: A yes-no data field is qualitative, whereas a number-value data field is quantitative.

quantity.e: From Middle English quantite, from Old French quantité, from Latin quantitās (“quantity”), from quantus (“how much”).
quantity.x: You have to choose between quantity and quality.

quantum.e: From Late Latin quantum, noun use of neuter form of Latin quantus (“how much”).
quantum.x: The reader will perhaps be curious to know the quantum of this present, but we cannot satisfy his curiosity.

quarantine.e: From Medieval Latin quarentena and quarentīna (“40-day period, Lent”) via Middle English quarentine, Norman quarenteine, French quarenteine, and Italian quarantina, via…
quarantine.x: The tourists were put in quarantine to ensure none of them would be able to spread the plague.

quark.e: Etymology 1 sense 1 (“subatomic particle”) was coined by the American physicist Murray Gell-Mann (1929–2019) in 1963, apparently an arbitrary word.

quarrel.e: From Middle English querele (“altercation, dispute; argument, debate; armed combat; trial by combat; basis for dispute, complaint; claim, legal suit; a lament.
quarrel.x: We got into a silly quarrel about what food to order.

quarrelsome.x: She's too quarrelsome to participate in a civil conversation.

quarry.e: From Middle English quarere, from Medieval Latin quarreria (1266), literally a “place where stones are squared”, from Old French quarrière (compare modern French…
quarry.x: Michelangelo personally quarried marble from the world-famous quarry at Carrara.

quart.e: From Middle English quart, quarte, from Old French quarte, carte, from Latin quartus (“one-fourth”). Cognate with Spanish cuarto (“quarter; room, quarters”).
quart.x: A tierce major is good against any other tierce; a quart minor is good against a tierce major.

quarterly.x: The arms of Hohenzollern is quarterly argent and sable.

quartermaster.e: From Middle English quartermayster, quartermaistre, equivalent to quarter + master. Perhaps reinforced by and merged with Dutch kwartiermeester, kwartier-meester.

quartet.e: From French quartette, from Italian quartetto. Doublet of cuarteto and quartetto.
quartet.x: The string quartet played some chamber music.

quartz.e: From German Quarz, from Middle High German (Central East German) quarz, twarc, from a West Slavic language [compare Polish twardy (“hard”), Czech tvrdý (“hard”)], from…
quartz.x: Subsequently, the old Malay brought him the present specimen in a state of torpidity, telling him he had found it in a cavity of the quartz reef.

quasar.e: Blend of quasi- + stellar, from quasi-stellar radio source. Coined by American astrophysicist Hong-Yee Chiu in 1964 in an article in Physics Today.

quell.x: The nation obeyed the call, rallied round the sovereign, and enabled him to quell the disaffected minority.

quench.e: From Middle English quenchen, from Old English cwenċan, from Proto-Germanic *kwankijaną.
quench.x: The library quenched her thirst for knowledge.

query.e: An anglicisation of quere, an obsolete variant form of Latin quaere, second-person singular present active imperative of quaerō (“seek, look for; ask”).
query.x: The teacher answered the student’s query concerning biosynthesis.

quest.e: From Middle English quest, queste; partly from Anglo-Norman queste, Old French queste (“acquisition, search, hunt”), and partly from their source, Latin quaesta…
quest.x: to rove in quest of game, of a lost child, of property, etc.

questionable.x: It is questionable if the universe is open or closed.

quetzal.e: Borrowed from Spanish quetzal, from Classical Nahuatl quetzalli (“brightly colored tail feather, quetzal feather”), from quetza (“to raise, lift”).
quetzal.x: This particular wild avocado species had beautiful small black fruits set in a red cap that made it easy for the quetzals to find them.

quibble.x: He harped on his quibble about how the dark red paint should be described as carmine rather than burgundy.

quicklime.e: From Middle English quyk lym; equivalent to quick + lime.

quickness.e: From Middle English quiknes, qwiknes, quyknesse, cwicnesse, equivalent to quick + -ness.
quickness.x: The quickness of the hand deceives the eye.

quicksand.e: From Middle English quyksande, from Old English cwecesand (“quicksand”), equivalent to quick (“living”) + sand.
quicksand.x: My feet were firmly lodged in the quicksand, and the more I struggled the more I sank into it.

quill.e: From late Middle English quyl, which is first attested in the early 15th century with the meanings "fragment of reed" and "shaft of a feather", probably from Low German…
quill.x: He picked up his quill and wrote a poem.

quilt.e: Inherited from Middle English quilte, quylte, from Anglo-Norman quilte and Old French coilte, cuilte (compare French couette), from Latin culcita. Doublet of quoit.
quilt.x: My grandmother is going to sew a quilt.

quinoa.e: Borrowed from Spanish quinua, from Quechua kinwa.
quinoa.x: The oldest archeological remains of domesticated quinoa date to 5000 BC (Tapia 1979).

quintal.e: Late Middle English, from Anglo-Norman quintal, from Middle French quintal, from Old French and Medieval Latin quintale and quintallus (“various medieval…
quintal.x: In UgSL, we find a complete set of forms for dual, trial, quadral and quintal in several paradigmatic contrasts.

quintessence.e: PIE word *pénkʷe From Middle English, borrowed from Middle French, from Medieval Latin quinta essentia (“fifth essence, aether”), equivalent to quint- + essence.

quintet.e: From French quintette, from Italian quintetto, diminutive of quinto (“fifth”), itself from Latin quintus, related to quīnque (“five”).
quintet.x: The composer wrote a string quintet in his early twenties.

quirk.e: First attested in the 1540s. Of uncertain origin. Possibly from Middle English *querk, from Old Norse kverk (“a bend or angle, especially below a cross-beam or below the…
quirk.x: The car steers cleanly, but the gearshift has a few quirks.

quiver.e: From Middle English quiver, from Anglo-Norman quivre, from Old Dutch cocare (source of Dutch koker, and cognate to Old English cocer (“quiver, case”)), from Proto-West…
quiver.x: Don Pedro: Nay, if Cupid have not spent all his quiver in Venice, thou wilt quake for this shortly.

quixotic.e: Derived from Spanish Quixote, the surname of Don Quixote, the title character in the novel by Miguel de Cervantes, + -ic.
quixotic.x: Olivier, as you know, was quixotic, and would not permit a secret service and spies.

quoll.e: From the earlier form je-quoll, from Guugu Yimidhirr dhigul. Recorded by Banks but then virtually forgotten for 150 years, with the term native cat used instead.

quorum.e: Inherited from Middle English quorum (c. 1426), from Anglo-Norman quorum, clipped from the Anglo-Latin wording of commissions in which certain persons were specially…
quorum.x: We can discuss the issue tonight but cannot vote until we have a quorum.

quota.e: From Latin quota pars; see Latin quota.

quotation.e: The obsolete sense of “quota”, from Medieval Latin quotātiō, from Latin quotāre, is attested from the 15th century.
quotation.x: "Where they burn books, they will also burn people" is a famous quotation from Heinrich Heine.

quotidian.e: From Anglo-Norman cotidian, cotidien, Middle French cotidian, cotidien, and their source, Latin cottīdiānus, quōtīdiānus (“happening every day”), from adverb cottīdiē…
quotidian.x: The story or the painting would serve to connect the part with the whole, the event with the myth, the quotidian with the sacred.

quotient.e: Borrowed from Latin quotiēns, from quotiēs.
quotient.x: Dividing 12 by 4 yields a quotient of 3.
